properties.decision:
RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. Anthony, 2026-08-14.

HIS WORDS, restating settled doctrine first and then adding the new part: *"we purposefully did not define every UAF/DoDAF view as those are not appropriate for every design project AND reflow2 was meant as 'design anything' and 'build anything' type construct. This is why I left rendering the reflow2 graph to be able to store any design structure/content and left the agent the responsible party for 'rendering' the drawing. It'd be like if I requested you to render me an OV-1 of reflow2 right now — you'd refer to the graph and pull what you need; then you'd build me a mermaid diagram or some html file or markdown file to show what the OV-1 is. That being said, sometimes not every systems engineering view is applicable to a given design. Feel like the agent should be able to also say, 'an OV-1 isn't applicable for your design; are you sure you want me to generate?'"*

═══ 📌 THE DOCTRINE THIS RESTS ON, RECORDED SO IT STOPS BEING RE-PROPOSED ═══

**THE UAF/DoDAF VIEW CATALOGUE IS DELIBERATELY NOT IN REFLOW2.** The division is: the GRAPH stores any design structure or content; the AGENT renders the drawing, in whatever medium suits — mermaid, HTML, markdown. Enumerating standard views inside reflow2 would bind a "design anything" tool to one discipline's catalogue, and `req:design-anything` (ACCEPTED) is the requirement that forbids it.
⚠️ **A SESSION PROPOSED EXACTLY THAT AN HOUR EARLIER** — option (c) of `dec:idea-a-view-can-slice-by-altitude-not-only-by-aspect` suggested rendering CV-1/CV-2/CV-3/AV-1 as first-class outputs. **Closed on his word.** It is recorded here because the pull toward hard-coding a familiar catalogue is strong and will recur.

═══ ⭐⭐ THE FINDING: APPLICABILITY AND INVENTION ARE THE SAME QUESTION ═══

`dec:views-are-projections` already holds that **a view is a projection of the graph and renderer fill-ins are DEFECTS**; `cap:bl-40` holds SYNTHESIZE to a no-extrapolation standard.

🛑 **NOW NOTICE WHAT "NOT APPLICABLE" ACTUALLY MEANS.** A view does not apply to a design precisely when the graph lacks the material that view projects from. And if the material is absent, **rendering it anyway REQUIRES the agent to invent the content** — which is the defect the doctrine already forbids. So:

  > *"Is this view applicable?"* and *"would drawing it force me to make things up?"* are **the same question asked at two different times.**

⇒ This is not a new principle. **It is the existing no-fill-in rule moved EARLIER — from a defect caught after the fact, to a question asked before the pen touches paper.** That reframing is what makes it worth building: the rule currently has no moment at which it is enforced, because the only party who could notice is the agent that is already mid-render and motivated to produce something.

⇒ AND IT MAKES APPLICABILITY COMPUTABLE RATHER THAN A JUDGEMENT. *"Does an OV-1 apply?"* is a matter of taste. *"Does this graph hold operational actors, activities and the exchanges between them, and how many?"* is a count. **The second is answerable by reflow2 without reflow2 ever knowing what an OV-1 is.**

═══ THE SHAPE THAT KEEPS THE CATALOGUE OUT ═══

The agent DECLARES the projection it intends to draw — the node types and edge types it will read. reflow2 answers with what it actually holds and what is absent. The agent then either renders, or says *"an OV-1 isn't applicable for your design; are you sure?"* **reflow2 never learns the view's name, so the catalogue stays with the agent and the counting stays with the graph.** That division is the same one `dec:three-party-checks` already sets: the LLM speaks, the graph counts, the human decides.

⚠️ AND IT MUST ASK, NEVER REFUSE. His wording is *"are you sure you want me to generate?"* — a warning with a way through, not a block. Consistent with `dec:ask-not-repair` and `dec:report-dont-judge`. A sparse view is sometimes exactly what the user wants to see; an empty OV-1 is itself a finding about the design.

OPTIONS, NONE CHOSEN.
(a) LEAVE IT TO THE AGENT — status quo. It can already look at the graph and judge. Counter: unrepeatable between sessions, and the party judging is the one being asked to produce a deliverable, which is the weakest possible position for saying "this cannot honestly be drawn".
(b) ⭐ REFLOW2 ANSWERS A DECLARED PROJECTION — the agent names node/edge types, reflow2 returns counts and absences. Keeps the catalogue out, makes the answer computable and repeatable. Counter: an agent can declare the wrong projection and get a confident answer to the wrong question.
(c) A SERVED SKILL carries the discipline — a render-a-view skill whose steps include checking the material before drawing. Cheapest, and consistent with skills being where disciplines live. Counter: it is another instruction, and `req:skill-use-survives-a-long-session` is the standing evidence that instructions lose to urgency.
(d) HARD-CODE PER-VIEW APPLICABILITY RULES. **CLOSED on Anthony's word** — this is the catalogue-in-reflow2 route `req:design-anything` forbids.

🛑 THE LIMIT WORTH STATING: material presence is necessary but not sufficient. A view can be structurally renderable and still be the wrong instrument for the domain — an OV-1 of a machine shop might have actors and activities to draw and still be a category error. **Counting cannot see that; only the human can.** So (b) at its best reports *"here is what I hold and what I lack"*, and the applicability verdict stays with the person — which is the same honest division reflow2 uses everywhere else.
properties.name: OPEN — should reflow2 be able to tell an agent that a requested view does not apply to this design, given "would rendering it require invention?" is the same question as "is it applicable?"
properties.rationale: Captured under the brainstorm skill. Recorded separately from the altitude-view node because they are separately answerable: reflow2 could learn to report what a declared projection would find without ever gaining an altitude view, and vice versa. The reason this is worth a node rather than a note is the equivalence at its centre — applicability and invention turn out to be one question asked at two times — which converts a matter of taste into a count, and gives the existing no-fill-in doctrine the enforcement moment it currently lacks. Anthony's restatement of why the view catalogue is deliberately absent is recorded here too, because a session proposed hard-coding it an hour earlier and the pull toward a familiar standard catalogue will recur.
